blocks.p: Word had reached Rei that a shrine keeper in the north of the ward was frightened and wanted someone to come. Rei walked to Higashi-Jūjō station in the noon heat and took the Keihin-Tōhoku line one stop north to Akabane. The train was nearly empty at that hour. An old woman sat with a bunch of chrysanthemums across her lap, wrapped in newspaper, the kind of flowers people take to graves. She held them carefully, the way someone holds a sleeping baby.

At Akabane he came out into a wall of heat. The station square was loud with shop music and the crossing signal's chirping. He left it behind and climbed into the quiet streets on the hill, where the houses were older and the lanes turned for no reason. Paper lanterns hung under the eaves, and in one doorway a family had set out a little horse made from a cucumber and four wooden sticks. At Obon some families make these. The fast cucumber horse is to bring the dead home quickly. A slow eggplant cow takes them back at the end of the week, so they can stay a little longer. Rei had made them as a child, with Gin.

blocks.cap: The Hozumi fox shrine in upper Kita

blocks.p: The shrine was at the top of a flight of worn stone steps. The old man was sweeping when Rei arrived, and that was the first wrong thing. The stones were already clean. He swept them anyway, slowly, back and forth over the same place, like a man keeping his hands busy so that they would not shake.

blocks.cap: Miyamoto Kazuo, head priest of the Hozumi shrine

blocks.p: His name was Miyamoto Kazuo. He was sixty-six, the head priest, a kannushi, which is what Shinto calls the man who looks after a shrine and speaks for it to its god. He wore white and indigo, and his white hair was tied in a small topknot. He told Rei who he was before Rei could ask. His father had kept this shrine before him, and his grandfather before that. His family had protected this ground for two hundred years. Every Obon someone in his family renewed the wards that ringed the grounds. He recited it the way a man reads out the deed to a house he is afraid is no longer his.

The shrine itself was almost nothing. It was a fox shrine, an Inari shrine. Inari is the Shinto god of rice and good harvests, and foxes are its messengers, so two stone foxes sat at the entrance with lichen grown into their grins. The gate was a torii, the simple two-post gateway that marks the line where the ordinary world ends and the god's ground begins. Its vermilion paint had faded to the colour of dried blood. An old camphor tree stood beside it, and Miyamoto bowed to the tree as he passed, out of a habit older than thought. Under a little roof stood a stone basin of still water, where visitors rinse their hands and mouths before they pray. A three-coloured cat sat on the rim of the basin and stared into it without drinking. It was the kind of place the city forgets so completely that the forgetting becomes a kind of protection.

Miyamoto would not let Rei near the basin until he had said what he had called him to say. He said it badly, in pieces, looking at the broom. For two hundred years the water in that basin had held the lanterns. Every Obon the neighbourhood strung paper lights along the lane, and every Obon the basin caught their reflection and held them, doubled and trembling on the surface. That reflection, Miyamoto said, was how a keeper knew the boundary was holding. A shrine that reflects is a shrine that is still listening.
"This week the lanterns are lit," he said. "The lane is strung. And the water lies there flat and black and holds nothing. No lights. No roof beam. When you lean over it, your own face is not there."

Both of Rei's registers came up at that, the low one and the searching one, slow and certain. For once they agreed. All week he had been learning one particular kind of wrongness, the wrongness of a thing that had stopped answering. Gin's flat. The address that was in no file. The cases closed too cleanly. He recognised the same shape in an old man's basin.

Miyamoto leaned the broom against the gate and took a packet of cigarettes from his sleeve. His hands shook too much for the match. Without thinking, Rei took out his lighter and held the flame for him. The old man drew on the cigarette, nodded his thanks, and seemed to steady.

"I am too old to read what has gone wrong," he said, "and too frightened to leave it unread. I sent word to the Division. The Division sent a form. I sent word to the temple. The temple sent prayers." He looked at Rei properly for the first time. "You are the only one who came up the steps instead of mailing something down them."
Rei asked him what the wards actually were. He knew how the CVD did it, with glyphs and grades and paperwork. This was not that.

"We do not fight what comes," Miyamoto said. "My father used to say Shinto does not exorcise so much as it tidies. Every night I walk the grounds. The lamps, the salt at the gate at dusk, the gate itself. I keep the place clean and named and in good repair, and things that should not cross find it does not want them. Once a year, at Obon, the cords are re-tied, and the water is asked to keep watching. That is all. It has been enough for two hundred years." He blew smoke toward the camphor tree, then apologised to it. "It has been enough until this week."

Up close, the water was worse than Miyamoto had described. He had described an empty thing, and empty is at least clean. This was not clean. The basin was full to the brim and perfectly still. No wind reached it under the little roof. When Rei leaned over it, the lanterns behind him did not appear, and neither did he. But the surface was not blank. Something was moving under it, very slowly, like something turning over far down in deep water. The basin was only a hand deep.
The cat stepped down from the rim and walked away from him with its tail low.

Rei put two fingers on the stone rim, not on the water, and let the read come. It came wrong. A shrine basin should taste of two hundred Obons of cupped hands and rinsed mouths and small honest wishes. This one tasted of all that. But underneath it, there was a single clean cut. Something that had been woven together had been carefully unwoven, by someone who knew exactly which thread to lift.

He crouched and looked longer than was wise. The longer he looked, the surer both registers became. The water was not failing to reflect him. It was choosing not to. Long ago, a boundary had been set here between the lane and whatever the lane was built to forget. The reflection kept that boundary tight. Every day the water proved that the world on this side was solid enough to throw an image back. Take away that proof, and the boundary goes slack.

Three steps behind him, the lanterns burned gold along the lane. At the rim of this stone, their light simply stopped, as if the basin had been excused from the evening. Someone had set it apart, quietly, so that it could be used without anyone in the neighbourhood noticing.

When he took his fingers off the rim, the movement under the surface settled, the way water settles after a fish has turned. For one moment before it went flat, the black water showed him a face after all. It was not his. It was a calm, pleasant, entirely reasonable face. He had been learning its shape all week without ever being allowed to see it clearly. Then the water lay still and gave him nothing.
"Did you see anything?" Miyamoto asked, in the small voice of a man who already knew.

The honest answer was that Rei had seen the Healer. It had dressed itself in a two-hundred-year-old shrine the way a doctor puts on a clean white coat, so that everyone would trust it. He said, "Yes." The lane kept burning. The basin kept its peace, and it was the wrong kind of peace. Someone had arranged it.

The shrine office was a tiny room behind the gate, one tatami mat wide. A thread of cedar smoke rose from a dish in the corner, as it had in this room, Miyamoto said, for as long as anyone remembered. The book of renewals was older than the light bulb and older than the table. It was really many books, bound by hand and stacked in a pile wrapped in cloth. Each one held a generation of Obons, written in the small cramped hand of whoever had held the broom that century.

Miyamoto turned to this year's page slowly, like a man opening a wound to show the doctor where it hurts. The entry was there, but in a handwriting Rei did not know. It was not Miyamoto's and not his family's. It was a clean modern script. In the place where the keeper records who renewed the wards, it had written one phrase. A friend assisted.

"He came in the spring," Miyamoto said, looking at the stranger's writing in his family's book. "A soft-spoken man. A healer, he said. He had heard the old keeper's hands were failing." He held up his own hands and let Rei see the tremor. "I have no one yet to pass the duty to. He knew that too. He offered, for nothing, for the simple rightness of it, to help me renew the work I could no longer manage alone." His voice broke a little, the way a voice does when a kindness turns out to have been a knife. "He was so very kind. He asked only that I let him tie the last knot himself. The last knot, he said, is the one that matters."

Rei read the entry, and both registers went cold and quiet. He knew this work. The same neatness. The same gift, offered into exactly the gap a person is most ashamed of. It was all through Gin's ledger of favours. It was everywhere he had been this week, wherever Yushiro the Healer had reached into someone's worst small fear and changed one thread while they cried with gratitude.

The wards had not been broken. They had been re-tied, expertly, by a guest the keeper had invited in himself, because he was ashamed of his failing hands. And the last knot, the one that held the reflection and kept the boundary listening, had been tied to give way at a planned time. This week. Obon, when the veil over all of Kita was at its thinnest, and every shrine in the district was straining to hold its own small piece of the wall. Pull one keeper's stone loose at a time like this and there is no flood. There is a draught. One clean current of cold air through one forgotten shrine, feeding the larger thinning the Healer had been working toward all along.

Miyamoto wanted to know what Rei would do. Underneath that, he wanted to know what he himself had done. Had his weak hands caused this? Or would it have come anyway? There was no answer Rei could give that would return to him that spring morning, when he had been so grateful to be helped.

Rei went back out and stood at the basin with his hands in his pockets. The temptation came quietly, and it spoke in a reasonable voice. The Healer did not know that he had found this. If he left the knot as it was, the shrine would go on failing on schedule. The small cold current through the water would show him exactly where the larger thinning ran and what it was for. He could sit on these steps every night until Obon ended and take notes. It would cost an old man his basin. It would cost a boundary his family had kept for two hundred years. And it would cost whatever else came through the draught while Rei stood beside it with a pencil.

blocks.cap: The three-coloured cat of the shrine

blocks.p: The cat came and sat beside his foot and looked up at him. Rei thought about Gin, who would have closed it without a second thought. Gin sat up all night with widows and wrote the case files afterwards. The voice that wanted the window left open sounded sensible, and that was exactly what frightened him. It was the Healer's kind of sum. A hole in a neighbourhood's wall, left open because the hole was useful. He would not learn to think like that.
"We close it," he said. "But first I need to read where it goes."

Miyamoto did not argue. He fetched the cords from the office. They were shimenawa, the sacred ropes Shinto uses to mark a holy place, made of twisted hemp with folded white paper strips hanging from them. He showed Rei the knots his father had taught him. Rei went back to the basin and put his whole hand flat on the stone this time. He let the current run through him for as long as he could bear it. It was cold and steady and it ran one way. North. Toward the river, and past it, toward the old ground beyond the freight line where the city's maps went vague. He held that direction in his mind like a compass bearing. Then he took his hand away.

The re-tying took the rest of the afternoon. Miyamoto's hands knew every knot and could not hold any of them steady. Rei's hands were steady and knew nothing. So Rei held the cords tight and the old man tied. When they reached the last knot, Rei ran his fingertips along the cord and found the place where the stranger had worked. One strand had been lifted loose and laid back in place so that it would slip. He showed Miyamoto. Miyamoto bowed to the camphor tree, then to the basin. Then he bent and tied the knot the way his father had tied it. It was a plain knot. It did not slip.

Evening came, as it always did on the third night of Obon. The neighbourhood came out. Old women walked by in yukata printed with blue morning glories and white waves. Children had fox masks from the festival stalls pushed up on their foreheads. They filed past the little shrine, clapped twice and bowed, and none of them felt the cold seam Rei had spent the day standing inside. That was the mercy and the horror of a forgotten shrine. When it failed, the only people who could not see it fail were the people it protected.

Then Miyamoto lit the last lantern at the gate, and the basin caught it. The light came back doubled and trembling on the water. Then the next lantern, and the next, until the whole gold string of the lane lay under the little roof the way it had lain for two hundred summers. The three-coloured cat jumped onto the rim, looked into the water, and drank.

Miyamoto found Rei at the gate and read his face the way old keepers read water. What passed between them was not exactly gratitude. Rei had not given him back the spring. Both of them knew that the kind stranger would come again, to some other pair of failing hands, with the same soft offer and the same patient knot. But the old man took Rei's hand in both of his. His hands were dry and light as paper.

"My father used to say the shrine does not protect the neighbourhood from the thing on the other side," he said. "It protects the thing on the other side from the neighbourhood's forgetting. It keeps it small and named and bounded. A forgotten thing grows. A watched thing waits."

Rei had brought back the watching. Somewhere across the thinning city, the Healer had lost one quiet draught. It was still one stone further along a wall it meant to bring down by the end of Obon. But Rei had something now that he had not had that morning. He knew which way the draught had been running.

He walked home the long way. He did not want a train. He went south down the hill and through the back streets, past small factories with their shutters down for the holiday, past a sentō, a public bath, with its tall chimney and the smell of hot water and soap drifting from its door. On a corner a group of men in undershirts sat on beer crates outside a liquor shop, talking quietly, fanning themselves. A vending machine glowed white in the dark beside them, and a moth beat against its glass. Every few streets there was a little altar at a doorway, a candle in a glass and a plate of fruit, set out for someone's dead. Rei had never noticed how many there were. This year he saw every one.

Near home he passed the small Inari shrine a hundred metres north of Gin's building. He had walked past it a thousand times without looking. Tonight he stopped. Gin had written about this shrine in the district pages of the archive, and Rei remembered the note now.

blocks.p: So that was part of why Gin did his writing at home. He had been sitting inside the shrine's quiet.

blocks.cap: Ishikawa Tsuneko, caretaker of Jūjō Inari

blocks.p: An old woman was refilling the lamp beside the fox statues. She was small and straight-backed, in a grey work apron, and she watched Rei come under the torii without any warmth at all. He did not speak first. He rinsed his hands at the basin. Then he bowed twice, clapped twice and bowed once more, the way he had been taught as a boy. Only then did he turn to her.

Her name was Ishikawa Tsuneko. She was seventy-one. She had kept Jūjō Inari for thirty-one years. Her grandmother had kept it before her, and her family had done the work here since the Meiji era, the years at the end of the nineteenth century when Japan first opened to the modern world. She did not call it ward work or symbol work. She called it the duties. Which nights needed the salt. Which corners needed the lamp. Which visitors were carrying something they should not have brought up the steps. She did not think of herself as a practitioner of anything. She only knew that the shrine worked.
Rei looked into her basin. The lanterns from the street were there, small and doubled and steady.
"Has anyone offered to help you with the duties?" he asked. "This year. Someone kind."

She gave him a long, measuring look. "The government has asked to help me three times," she said. "I said no. The other ones, the ones without an office, have asked twice. I said no to them too." She put her hand on the rim of the basin. When she lifted it, Rei felt that the stone was warmer than the evening, as if she had left something of herself in it. "I do not let anyone else do the duties. A thing you hand to a stranger is not your duty any more."

Gin's archive said that the people without an office, the Grid, had decided to leave her alone. Her work was the reason this corner of Jūjō had stayed steady for decades, and if they interfered with her they would break something they relied on. Rei suspected she knew that. He suspected she would never say so.

He thanked her and went down the steps as drums started somewhere toward the river. It was the slow, heavy rhythm of a bon odori, the Obon dance, when the neighbourhood dances in a circle under lanterns to welcome the dead home for their three nights and then send them off again. The sound found the tight thing in Rei that had been pulled hard all day, and loosened it a little. Down at the embankment the first paper lantern boats were going onto the black water, each one carrying a small candle out for the dead. The dead were very close this week. And they were getting closer by exactly as many stones as the Healer could talk a grieving keeper into loosening. Tonight there was one stone fewer. And there were two old people in Kita who would not hand their duty to anyone.
